subject: Cloud Computing
title: Backup and Disaster Recovery for Data
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Backup and Disaster Recovery for Data.

hook.text: GitLab lost six hours of production data in 2017. Five backup methods failed. Only one partial backup worked.

buildup.text: Cloud backups should follow the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, on two different media, with one copy offsite.

discovery.text: Cross-region backups protect against regional outages. Cross-account backups protect against account compromise.

twist.text: Backups are worthless if never tested. Many teams discover broken backups only during an actual disaster.

climax.text: Cloud makes backups easy to automate. But automation without verification is just a false sense of security.

punchline.text: Backup is not the goal. Successful restore is the goal.

quiz.question: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?
options: Three copies, on two different media types, with one copy stored offsite
Back up three times a day, twice a week, once a month
Three servers, two regions, one cloud provider

details.summary: Cloud data backup strategies include automated snapshots, cross-region replication, and point-in-time recovery. The right approach depends on RPO and RTO requirements. Managed databases automate most backup tasks, but responsibility for testing restores remains with the customer.
details.whyItMatters: Backups are worthless if they cannot be restored. Regular restore testing is the most neglected practice in cloud data management and the first thing that fails during a real disaster.
takeaways: Cross-region replication protects against regional failures
Restore testing is essential but frequently neglected

faq.question: How often should you test database restores?
faq.answer: At least quarterly for production databases, monthly for critical systems. Automated restore testing in a separate environment can run weekly or even daily. The test should verify not just that the restore completes but that the data is consistent and the application works.

faq.question: What is point-in-time recovery?
faq.answer: Point-in-time recovery lets you restore a database to any second within a retention window, typically up to 35 days. It uses continuous backup of transaction logs. This is critical for recovering from accidental deletions or corrupt data writes.
